Drawing on twelve semi\u2010structured interviews conducted across homes, workplaces, and caf\u00e9s in the city, seven of which anchor the primary analysis presented here, it employs a feminist political economy lens and interpretivist methodology to foreground care as a contested terrain rather than a normative moral duty. The analysis reveals how women's labor is organized through moral economies, gendered spatialities, and temporal dispossession, producing forms of exhaustion that are routinized and affectively sanctioned. It situates self\u2010care not as commodified wellness but as a relational act of micro\u2010resistance, theorized through decolonial and affective feminist frameworks. By centering participant testimony, this article reorients care from moral virtue to political struggle, calling for a reconfiguration of care ethics rooted in collective infrastructures that refuse neoliberal logics of self\u2010responsibilities and opening new epistemological imaginaries for feminist urban
